notes.front: What is hypoxia?
notes.back: A state of oxygen deficiency in the body sufficient to impair the functions of the brain and other organs.
notes.explanation: The greatest concern in flight is the brain, which is particularly vulnerable to oxygen deprivation; any reduction in mental function can lead to life-threatening errors.
notes.example: Like a candle in a jar with the lid on: it keeps burning for a while, but ever more weakly as the oxygen runs short.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, chapter 8, section 1, “8-1-2 Effects of Altitude”
notes.evidence: Hypoxia is a state of oxygen deficiency in the body sufficient to impair functions of the brain and other organs.

notes.front: What is hypoxic hypoxia?
notes.back: Hypoxia caused by insufficient oxygen available to the body as a whole, such as the lower partial pressure of oxygen at altitude.
notes.explanation: The percentage of oxygen stays the same as the aircraft climbs, but fewer oxygen molecules are available at the pressure needed to pass into the blood.
notes.example: Like trying to fill a bucket from a tap with low water pressure: the water is the same, but less of it gets through.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 17, “Hypoxic Hypoxia”, p. 17-3
notes.evidence: Hypoxic hypoxia is a result of insufficient oxygen available

notes.front: What is hypemic hypoxia?
notes.back: Hypoxia in which the blood cannot take up and carry enough oxygen to the cells, even though enough is breathed in.
notes.explanation: “Hypemic” means “not enough blood”; the cause is a deficiency in the blood, not a lack of inhaled oxygen.
notes.example: Like a delivery firm with plenty of parcels but too few working vans to carry them.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 17, “Hypemic Hypoxia”, p. 17-3

notes.front: What is stagnant hypoxia?
notes.back: Hypoxia in which oxygen-rich blood is not flowing to the tissues that need it.
notes.explanation: “Stagnant” means “not flowing”; an arm or leg “going to sleep” because its blood flow was cut off is one form.
notes.example: Like a traffic jam on the only road into town: the goods exist, but they are not moving to where they are needed.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 17, “Stagnant Hypoxia”, p. 17-3

notes.front: What is histotoxic hypoxia?
notes.back: Hypoxia in which enough oxygen reaches the cells, but they cannot make use of it.
notes.explanation: “Histo” refers to tissues or cells and “toxic” means poisonous; the impairment can be caused by alcohol and other drugs, such as narcotics and poisons.
notes.example: Like a factory that receives every delivery but whose machines are jammed, so nothing gets used.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 17, “Histotoxic Hypoxia”, p. 17-4

notes.front: What is time of useful consciousness (TUC)?
notes.back: The maximum time a pilot has to make rational, life-saving decisions and carry them out at a given altitude without supplemental oxygen.
notes.explanation: As altitude increases above 10,000 feet, hypoxia symptoms grow more severe and the time of useful consciousness rapidly decreases.
notes.example: Like the time you can hold your breath under water: you can still act, but only for so long, and less the deeper you go.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 17, “Treatment of Hypoxia”, p. 17-4

notes.front: What is spatial disorientation?
notes.back: A lack of orientation with regard to the position, attitude or movement of the aeroplane in space.
notes.explanation: The brain combines vestibular, somatosensory and visual information; flying can make these systems disagree, which can lead to disorientation.
notes.example: Like stepping off a spinning fairground ride: your body insists you are still turning while your eyes say you have stopped.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 17, “Spatial Disorientation and Illusions”, p. 17-6
notes.evidence: orientation with regard to the position, attitude, or movement

notes.front: What is the vestibular system?
notes.back: The organs in the inner ear that sense movement and orientation, including three semicircular canals at roughly right angles to each other.
notes.explanation: Acceleration deflects fine hairs in the fluid-filled canals, which sends nerve impulses to the brain; without an outside visual reference it becomes unreliable.
notes.example: Like a spirit level with three bubbles, one for each direction, built into your head.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 17, “Spatial Disorientation and Illusions”, p. 17-6
notes.evidence: sense movement and determine orientation in the surrounding

notes.front: What is “the leans”?
notes.back: An illusion of banking the opposite way after levelling the wings from a gradual, prolonged turn that went unnoticed.
notes.explanation: The pilot may lean in the direction of the original turn to regain a sense of being upright; it is the most common illusion in flight.
notes.example: Like sitting in a train that slowly curves: when it straightens, you feel it tilting the other way.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 17, “Vestibular Illusions: The Leans”, p. 17-7

notes.front: What is the graveyard spiral?
notes.back: An illusion in a prolonged, coordinated constant-rate turn of being in a wings-level descent, which leads the pilot to pull back and tighten the spiral.
notes.explanation: The pilot feels no turn, only the loss of altitude; pulling back on the controls increases the loss of altitude and may lead to loss of control.
notes.example: Like tightening a corkscrew while believing you are pulling it straight out.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 17, “Graveyard Spiral”, p. 17-7

notes.front: What is the Coriolis illusion?
notes.back: An illusion of turning or accelerating on a different axis, caused by moving the head in a prolonged turn after the inner-ear fluid has settled.
notes.explanation: The disoriented pilot may manoeuvre the aircraft into a dangerous attitude trying to correct a movement that is not happening.
notes.example: Like spinning on an office chair, then nodding your head: the room seems to tumble in a new direction.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 17, “Coriolis Illusion”, p. 17-7
notes.evidence: of turning or accelerating on an entirely different axis.

notes.front: What is the somatogravic illusion?
notes.back: The illusion, from a rapid acceleration such as takeoff, of being in a nose-up attitude.
notes.explanation: The acceleration stimulates the otolith organs in the same way as tilting the head backwards, especially when visual references are poor.
notes.example: Like being pressed back into your seat in a fast car and feeling as if it is climbing a hill.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 17, “Somatogravic Illusion”, p. 17-7
notes.evidence: A rapid acceleration, such as experienced during takeoff

notes.front: What is the inversion illusion?
notes.back: The illusion of tumbling backwards, caused by an abrupt change from a climb to straight-and-level flight.
notes.explanation: The abrupt change stimulates the otolith organs strongly enough to create the feeling.
notes.example: Like the stomach-lifting feeling at the crest of a roller coaster, interpreted as falling over backwards.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 17, “Inversion Illusion”, p. 17-8
notes.evidence: An abrupt change from climb to straight-and-level flight can

notes.front: What is the elevator illusion?
notes.back: The illusion of being in a climb, caused by an abrupt upward vertical acceleration such as an updraft.
notes.explanation: An abrupt downward acceleration, usually in a downdraft, has the opposite effect.
notes.example: Like the feeling in a lift that starts upwards suddenly, but in a cockpit with no floor numbers to check.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 17, “Elevator Illusion”, p. 17-8

notes.front: What is carbon monoxide poisoning?
notes.back: Hypemic hypoxia caused by carbon monoxide, a colourless, odourless gas from internal combustion engines, attaching to the haemoglobin in the blood.
notes.explanation: The gas attaches to haemoglobin about 200 times more easily than oxygen, so the blood cannot carry oxygen to the cells.
notes.example: Like counterfeit passengers taking every seat on a bus so that the real passengers are left behind.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 17, “Carbon Monoxide (CO) Poisoning”, p. 17-12
notes.evidence: CO is a colorless and odorless gas produced by all internal

notes.front: What is motion sickness?
notes.back: Airsickness caused by the brain receiving conflicting messages about the state of the body.
notes.explanation: Symptoms include discomfort, nausea, dizziness, paleness, sweating and vomiting; it generally goes away within the first few lessons.
notes.example: Like reading in the back of a car on a winding road: your eyes say still, your inner ear says moving, and you feel ill.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 17, “Motion Sickness”, p. 17-12
notes.evidence: receiving conflicting messages about the state of the body.

notes.front: What is an ear block?
notes.back: A pressure difference between the middle ear and the cabin large enough to hold the eustachian tube closed, so the ear cannot equalise.
notes.explanation: Congestion from a cold, sore throat or nasal allergy can cause it, and it produces severe ear pain and loss of hearing.
notes.example: Like a stuck valve on a bicycle tyre: pressure builds on one side and nothing lets it through.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, chapter 8, section 1, “8-1-2 Effects of Altitude, Ear Block”
notes.evidence: the difference in pressure between the middle ear and aircraft cabin can build up to a level that will hold the eustachian tube closed, making equalization difficult if not impossible. The problem is commonly referred to as an “ear block.”

notes.front: What is a sinus block?
notes.back: Congestion that plugs the small openings between the sinuses and nasal passages, so sinus pressure cannot equalise with the cabin.
notes.explanation: It usually produces excruciating pain over the sinus area and occurs most frequently during descent.
notes.example: Like a sealed jar carried down a mountain: the pressure outside rises and presses on it, with nowhere to equalise.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, chapter 8, section 1, “8-1-2 Effects of Altitude, Sinus Block”
notes.evidence: This “sinus block” occurs most frequently during descent.

notes.front: What is decompression sickness (DCS)?
notes.back: Symptoms caused when low barometric pressure makes inert gases, mainly nitrogen, dissolved in body fluids and tissues come out of solution as bubbles.
notes.explanation: It can happen when flying an unpressurised aircraft to altitude or in a rapid decompression; the most common symptom is joint pain, “the bends”.
notes.example: Like opening a fizzy drink: the dissolved gas forms bubbles as soon as the pressure drops.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 17, “Altitude-Induced Decompression Sickness (DCS)”, p. 17-18
notes.evidence: tissues, to come out of physical solution and form bubbles.

notes.front: What is hypothermia?
notes.back: Body temperature that is too low.
notes.explanation: Body temperature reflects the balance between the heat the body produces and the heat it loses, and even mild hypothermia can compromise the safety of a flight.
notes.example: At first the only sign is shivering, but as core body temperature drops a pilot may be impaired while still feeling alert.
notes.source: FAA, Federal Air Surgeon, “Aeromedical Advisory: A Pilot’s Guide to Hypothermia and Hyperthermia”, Cleared for Takeoff blog
notes.evidence: a refresher on hypothermia (body temperature too low) and hyperthermia (body temperature too high) seems appropriate

notes.front: What is empty-field myopia?
notes.back: The eyes relaxing to a focus of 10 to 30 feet when nothing outside gives them a target, so the pilot looks without seeing.
notes.explanation: It usually occurs when flying above the clouds or in a haze layer.
notes.example: Like staring at a blank wall and realising your eyes have drifted out of focus without your noticing.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 17, “Empty-Field Myopia”, p. 17-22
notes.evidence: Empty-field myopia is a condition that usually occurs when flying above the clouds or in a haze layer that provides nothing specific to focus on outside the aircraft.

notes.front: What are personal minimums?
notes.back: Limits a pilot sets for each risk category that are unique to that pilot’s current level of experience and proficiency.
notes.explanation: They mark the difference between what is “legal” under the regulations and what is “smart” or “safe” for that pilot.
notes.example: Like a new driver deciding not to drive on motorways at night yet, although the licence allows it.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 2, “The PAVE Checklist”, p. 2-8
notes.evidence: for items in each risk category. These are limits unique to that

notes.front: What is get-there-itis?
notes.back: An operational pitfall in which fixation on the original goal or destination, with disregard for any alternative, impairs the pilot’s judgement.
notes.explanation: The handbook lists it among the operational pitfalls and, with “get-home-itis” and “let’s-go-itis”, among the external pressures on a flight.
notes.example: Like driving on through a worsening snowstorm because you promised to be home for dinner.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 2, “Operational Pitfalls (Figure 2-15)”, p. 2-22
notes.evidence: This disposition impairs pilot judgment through a fixation on the original goal or destination, combined with a disregard for any alternative course of action.

notes.front: At altitude the air is still about 21 percent oxygen. What, then, causes altitude hypoxia?
notes.back: Only the reduced barometric pressure at altitude.
notes.explanation: The oxygen concentration stays about 21 percent from the ground out to space; it is the pressure that falls.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, chapter 8, section 1, “8-1-2 Effects of Altitude”
notes.evidence: Hypoxia from exposure to altitude is due only to the reduced barometric pressures encountered at altitude, for the concentration of oxygen in the atmosphere remains about 21 percent from the ground out to space.

notes.front: From what cabin pressure altitude can night vision start to deteriorate from hypoxia?
notes.back: As low as 5,000 feet.
notes.explanation: Other significant effects usually do not occur in a normal healthy pilot below 12,000 feet.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, chapter 8, section 1, “8-1-2 Effects of Altitude”
notes.evidence: Although a deterioration in night vision occurs at a cabin pressure altitude as low as 5,000 feet, other significant effects of altitude hypoxia usually do not occur in the normal healthy pilot below 12,000 feet.

notes.front: For optimum protection, above what altitudes does the Aeronautical Information Manual encourage supplemental oxygen by day and at night?
notes.back: Above 10,000 feet by day and above 5,000 feet at night.
notes.explanation: The regulations demand less: crew must use oxygen after 30 minutes at cabin altitudes between 12,500 and 14,000 feet, and at once above 14,000 feet.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, chapter 8, section 1, “8-1-2 Effects of Altitude”
notes.evidence: For optimum protection, pilots are encouraged to use supplemental oxygen above 10,000 feet during the day, and above 5,000 feet at night.

notes.front: What is the treatment for hypoxia?
notes.back: Flying at lower altitudes and/or using supplemental oxygen.
notes.explanation: All pilots are susceptible, regardless of physical endurance or acclimatisation.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 17, “Treatment of Hypoxia”, p. 17-4
notes.evidence: Treatment for hypoxia includes flying at lower altitudes and/

notes.front: Which hypoxia symptom shows as blue fingernails and lips?
notes.back: Cyanosis.
notes.explanation: It is one of the common symptoms the handbook lists, with headache, impaired judgement and drowsiness among others.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 17, “Symptoms of Hypoxia”, p. 17-4
notes.evidence: Cyanosis (blue fingernails and lips)

notes.front: Which feelings can be among the first symptoms of hypoxia?
notes.back: Euphoria and a carefree feeling.
notes.explanation: With increasing oxygen starvation, the extremities become less responsive and flying becomes less coordinated.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 17, “Symptoms of Hypoxia”, p. 17-4
notes.evidence: can include euphoria and a carefree feeling.

notes.front: As hypoxia worsens, what happens to the pilot’s field of vision?
notes.back: It begins to narrow, and interpreting the instruments can become difficult.
notes.explanation: The handbook notes that the symptoms of hypoxia vary with the individual.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 17, “Symptoms of Hypoxia”, p. 17-4

notes.front: Why can a hypoxic pilot fail to act even when symptoms are present?
notes.back: Hypoxia can give a false sense of security, deceiving the pilot into believing everything is normal.
notes.explanation: Symptoms also vary between individuals, which is why an altitude chamber flight helps pilots learn their own.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 17, “Symptoms of Hypoxia”, p. 17-4

notes.front: Cruising at 13,500 feet without oxygen, you notice you feel cheerful and carefree and keep misreading the chart. What should you do?
notes.back: B) Suspect hypoxia: descend and/or use supplemental oxygen.
notes.choices:
A) Carry on: feeling good shows you are fit to fly
B) Suspect hypoxia: descend and/or use supplemental oxygen
C) Breathe faster to take in more oxygen
notes.choicesExplained: A: euphoria can be an early hypoxia symptom and gives a false sense of security. C: breathing faster tends to lead to hyperventilation, not recovery.
notes.explanation: Euphoria and impaired judgement are hypoxia symptoms, and the treatment is lower altitude and/or supplemental oxygen.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 17, “Symptoms of Hypoxia”, p. 17-4
notes.evidence: can include euphoria and a carefree feeling

notes.front: According to research the handbook cites, one ounce of alcohol can equal how much additional physiological altitude?
notes.back: About 2,000 feet.
notes.explanation: Alcohol causes histotoxic hypoxia by interfering with the cells’ use of oxygen.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 17, “Histotoxic Hypoxia”, p. 17-4
notes.evidence: equate to an additional 2,000 feet of physiological altitude.

notes.front: A pilot gave blood yesterday and flies today. Which type of hypoxia is the risk?
notes.back: Hypemic hypoxia.
notes.explanation: Blood donation reduces blood volume, which can take several weeks to recover; the blood carries less oxygen.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 17, “Hypemic Hypoxia”, p. 17-3

notes.back: Hypoxic hypoxia.
notes.explanation: The reduced partial pressure of oxygen at high altitude is the handbook’s example for pilots.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 17, “Hypoxic Hypoxia”, p. 17-3

notes.back: Histotoxic hypoxia.
notes.explanation: Alcohol interferes with the brain’s ability to use oxygen, producing a form of histotoxic hypoxia.

notes.front: According to the handbook’s table, roughly what is the time of useful consciousness at 25,000 feet MSL?
notes.back: 3 to 5 minutes.
notes.explanation: The same table gives 30 to 60 seconds at 35,000 feet, showing how quickly the time shrinks with altitude.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 17, “Figure 17-1. Time of useful consciousness”, p. 17-4
notes.evidence: 25,000 feet MSL 3 to 5 minutes

notes.front: What is both the best prevention and the best cure for hyperventilation?
notes.back: Breathing normally.
notes.explanation: Breathing into a paper bag or talking aloud also helps restore the body’s carbon dioxide level; recovery is usually rapid.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 17, “Hyperventilation”, p. 17-5
notes.evidence: normally is both the best prevention and the best cure for hyperventilation.

notes.front: Using an oxygen system, you develop symptoms that could be hypoxia or hyperventilation. What should you do first?
notes.back: Set the regulator to 100 percent oxygen and check the system is working, before attending to your breathing.
notes.explanation: Early symptoms of the two are similar and they can occur at the same time.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, chapter 8, section 1, “8-1-3 Hyperventilation in Flight”
notes.evidence: Therefore, if a pilot is using an oxygen system when symptoms are experienced, the oxygen regulator should immediately be set to deliver 100 percent oxygen, and then the system checked to assure that it has been functioning effectively before giving attention to rate and depth of breathing.

notes.front: At 3,000 feet, a nervous student starts breathing quickly and reports tingling fingers and light-headedness. What is the best first remedy?
notes.back: C) Slow the breathing rate, for example by talking aloud.
notes.choices:
A) Climb to get more oxygen
B) Breathe faster and deeper
C) Slow the breathing rate, for example by talking aloud
notes.choicesExplained: A: at 3,000 feet the rapid breathing, not altitude, is the problem, and climbing does not slow it. B: faster breathing blows off more carbon dioxide and worsens hyperventilation.
notes.explanation: Rapid breathing under stress leads to hyperventilation, and restoring a normal breathing rate is the cure.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 17, “Hyperventilation”, p. 17-5

notes.front: Why is equalising ear pressure more of a problem in descent than in the climb?
notes.back: In the climb the expanding air escapes down the eustachian tube by itself; in descent the pilot must periodically open the tube.
notes.explanation: This can be done by swallowing, yawning or tensing the throat muscles, or by the Valsalva manoeuvre.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, chapter 8, section 1, “8-1-2 Effects of Altitude, Ear Block”
notes.evidence: But during descent, the pilot must periodically open the eustachian tube to equalize pressure.

notes.front: If swallowing or yawning does not clear the ears in descent, what manoeuvre does the Aeronautical Information Manual describe?
notes.back: The Valsalva manoeuvre: close the mouth, pinch the nose closed and try to blow through the nostrils.
notes.explanation: Swallowing, yawning or tensing the throat muscles are the first things to try.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, chapter 8, section 1, “8-1-2 Effects of Altitude, Ear Block”
notes.evidence: or if these do not work, by a combination of closing the mouth, pinching the nose closed, and attempting to blow through the nostrils (Valsalva maneuver).

notes.front: How are ear and sinus blocks prevented, and are decongestant sprays a reliable answer?
notes.back: By not flying with an upper respiratory infection or nasal allergy; decongestant sprays or drops usually do not give adequate protection.
notes.explanation: Oral decongestants have side effects that can impair pilot performance.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, chapter 8, section 1, “8-1-2 Effects of Altitude, Ear Block”
notes.evidence: An ear block is prevented by not flying with an upper respiratory infection or nasal allergic condition. Adequate protection is usually not provided by decongestant sprays or drops to reduce congestion around the eustachian tubes.

notes.front: You have a heavy cold but feel well enough to fly. A friend suggests a decongestant nasal spray and going anyway. What is the sound decision?
notes.back: A) Do not fly until the cold has cleared.
notes.choices:
A) Do not fly until the cold has cleared
B) Fly, using the spray just before descent
C) Fly, but take an oral decongestant instead
notes.choicesExplained: B: sprays usually do not give adequate protection against a block. C: oral decongestants have side effects that can impair pilot performance.
notes.explanation: Ear and sinus blocks are prevented by not flying with an upper respiratory infection.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, chapter 8, section 1, “8-1-2 Effects of Altitude, Ear Block”
notes.evidence: An ear block is prevented by not flying with an upper respiratory infection or nasal allergic condition.

notes.front: Which three body systems work together to sense orientation?
notes.back: The vestibular, somatosensory and visual systems.
notes.explanation: Most of the time the three agree; flying can make them supply conflicting information.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 17, “Spatial Disorientation and Illusions”, p. 17-6
notes.evidence: systems that work together to ascertain orientation and

notes.front: Why can a pilot become disoriented quickly on entering cloud?
notes.back: With visual cues removed, false sensations from the other senses are no longer overruled by the eyes.
notes.explanation: In visual conditions the eyes are the major orientation source and usually prevail over false sensations.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 17, “Spatial Disorientation and Illusions”, p. 17-6
notes.evidence: these visual cues are removed, as they are in instrument

notes.front: Which three motions do the semicircular canals sense?
notes.back: Roll, pitch and yaw.
notes.explanation: The canals lie in three planes, at approximately right angles to each other.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 17, “Figure 17-3”, p. 17-6
notes.evidence: The semicircular canals lie in three planes and sense motions of roll, pitch, and yaw.

notes.front: Why can a pilot fail to notice the gradual turn that later causes the leans?
notes.back: Rotation at 2 degrees per second or less is below the detection threshold of the semicircular canals.
notes.explanation: So the turn goes unnoticed, and levelling the wings then feels like a bank the other way.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 17, “The Leans”, p. 17-7
notes.evidence: degrees per second or lower is below the detection threshold

notes.front: How can a pilot reduce the risk of the Coriolis illusion?
notes.back: Use an instrument scan with minimal head movement, and pick up dropped objects without sudden head movements.
notes.explanation: Moving the head in a different plane during a prolonged turn is what sets the inner-ear fluid moving.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 17, “Coriolis Illusion”, p. 17-7
notes.evidence: For this reason, it is important that pilots develop an instrument cross-check or scan that involves minimal head movement.

notes.front: In a graveyard spiral, what does the disoriented pilot do, and what is the result?
notes.back: Pulls back on the controls to stop the apparent descent, which tightens the spiral and increases the loss of altitude.
notes.explanation: The pilot feels no turn, so the altitude loss seems like a wings-level descent.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, chapter 8, section 1, “8-1-5 Illusions in Flight”
notes.evidence: The disoriented pilot will pull back on the controls, tightening the spiral and increasing the loss of altitude.

notes.front: What does the handbook call the most important way to cope with spatial disorientation?
notes.back: Become proficient in the flight instruments and rely on them: trust the instruments and disregard your sensory perceptions.
notes.explanation: The false sensations cannot be completely prevented, but training lets pilots ignore or suppress them.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 17, “Coping with Spatial Disorientation”, p. 17-10
notes.evidence: flight instruments and rely upon them. Trust the

notes.back: Reduced visibility, or at night when the horizon is not visible.
notes.explanation: The handbook says prevention is usually the best remedy for spatial disorientation.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 17, “Spatial Disorientation and Illusions”, p. 17-6

notes.front: After a long, very gentle left turn in cloud that you did not notice, you level the wings and feel strongly banked to the right. What is this, and what should you do?
notes.back: A) The leans: believe the attitude indicator and keep the wings level.
notes.choices:

notes.front: What is the most common symptom of DCS, and what is it called?
notes.back: Joint pain, known as “the bends”.
notes.explanation: It occurs when dissolved nitrogen leaves solution too rapidly and forms bubbles, mostly in the large joints.

notes.front: What should you do if altitude-induced DCS occurs in flight?
notes.back: Put on an oxygen mask at 100 percent, begin an emergency descent and land as soon as possible, then seek medical evaluation.
notes.explanation: The handbook says to land and be evaluated even if the symptoms disappear during descent.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 17, “Altitude-Induced Decompression Sickness (DCS)”, p. 17-18
notes.evidence: Put on oxygen mask immediately and switch the regulator to 100 percent oxygen.

notes.front: After a dive that did not need a controlled ascent, how long should you wait before flying at altitudes up to 8,000 feet?
notes.back: At least 12 hours.
notes.explanation: Diving lets more nitrogen dissolve in the body, which must be given time to leave before the pressure drops in flight.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, chapter 8, section 1, “8-1-2 Effects of Altitude, Decompression Sickness After Scuba Diving”

notes.front: After a dive that required a controlled ascent (decompression stops), how long should you wait before flying at altitudes up to 8,000 feet?
notes.back: At least 24 hours.
notes.explanation: The recommended altitudes are actual flight altitudes above mean sea level, not cabin altitudes.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, chapter 8, section 1, “8-1-2 Effects of Altitude, Decompression Sickness After Scuba Diving”
notes.evidence: and at least 24 hours after diving that required a controlled ascent (i.e., decompression stop diving).

notes.back: At least 24 hours.

notes.front: How can a pilot prevent empty-field myopia?
notes.back: By searching out and focusing on distant light sources, however dim; effective scanning also helps.
notes.explanation: The eyes otherwise relax to a focal distance of 10 to 30 feet, which means looking without seeing.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 17, “Empty-Field Myopia”, p. 17-22
notes.evidence: Searching out and focusing on distant light sources, no matter how dim, helps prevent the onset of empty-field myopia.

notes.front: In an effective traffic scan, how far should each eye movement be, and how long should each area be observed?
notes.back: No more than 10 degrees per movement, observing each area for at least 1 second.
notes.explanation: Only the small central fovea sends sharply focused images, so the sky is brought into central vision in short, regular steps.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, chapter 8, section 1, “8-1-6 Vision in Flight”
notes.evidence: Each movement should not exceed 10 degrees, and each area should be observed for at least 1 second to enable detection.

notes.front: According to studies the Aeronautical Information Manual cites, how should time be split between the instrument panel and outside?
notes.back: No more than 4 to 5 seconds on the panel for every 16 seconds outside.
notes.explanation: Time inside should be no more than a quarter to a third of the time spent scanning outside.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, chapter 8, section 1, “8-1-6 Vision in Flight”
notes.evidence: or no more than 4 to 5 seconds on the instrument panel for every 16 seconds outside.

notes.front: Flying VFR near a busy airport, which scanning method follows the Aeronautical Information Manual?
notes.back: A) Short, regularly spaced eye movements of up to 10 degrees, pausing about a second on each area.

B) One slow continuous sweep of the whole horizon without stopping

notes.choicesExplained: B: without pauses the eyes do not bring each area into sharp central vision long enough to detect traffic. C: time inside should be no more than a quarter to a third of time outside.
notes.explanation: Because only the fovea gives sharp vision, scanning in short steps with brief pauses is what lets the eye detect other aircraft.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, chapter 8, section 1, “8-1-6 Vision in Flight”
notes.evidence: effective scanning is accomplished with a series of short, regularly spaced eye movements that bring successive areas of the sky into the central visual field.

notes.back: A) Do not go (or wait): you set your limit where legal and safe for you differ.
notes.choices:
A) Do not go (or wait): you set your limit where legal and safe for you differ
B) Go: the flight is legal
C) Lower your personal minimum today, since the weather is only slightly worse
notes.choicesExplained: B: legal is not the same as smart or safe for your experience. C: minimums are set on the ground, away from the pressure of a particular trip.
notes.explanation: Personal minimums exist precisely for cases where the regulations permit something your experience does not yet support.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 2, “The PAVE Checklist”, p. 2-8
notes.evidence: of the regulations, and what is “smart” or “safe” in terms of pilot experience and proficiency.

notes.front: What are the five Ps of the 5P check?
notes.back: The Plan, the Plane, the Pilot, the Passengers and the Programming.
notes.explanation: They are reviewed at key decision points: preflight, before takeoff, midway, before descent and before the pattern.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 2, “The 5 Ps Check”, p. 2-13

notes.front: In the 5P concept, what are the easiest and second-easiest points to make a critical go/no-go decision?
notes.back: Easiest: preflight, before walking out to the aircraft. Second: just before takeoff.
notes.explanation: The handbook calls these two the critical go/no-go points on every flight.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 2, “The 5 Ps Check”, p. 2-13
notes.evidence: pilot and passengers walk out the door and load the aircraft.

notes.front: Planning a cross-country in the flight planning room, you see the destination forecast getting worse. Using the 5P concept, when is it easiest to cancel?
notes.back: A) Now, before you and your passengers walk out to the aircraft.
notes.choices:
A) Now, before you and your passengers walk out to the aircraft
B) At the run-up, once the engine is warm
C) At the midpoint, when destination weather comes into radio range
notes.choicesExplained: B: just before takeoff is only the second-easiest point. C: by the midpoint, many good options have already passed behind the aircraft.
notes.explanation: The first 5P decision point is preflight, where all the information and ways to make other travel plans are readily available.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 2, “The 5 Ps Check”, p. 2-13
notes.evidence: So the first decision point is preflight in the flight planning

notes.front: In the handbook’s IMSAFE checklist, what two time questions does the Alcohol item ask?
notes.back: “Have I been drinking within 8 hours? Within 24 hours?”
notes.explanation: As little as one ounce of liquor, one bottle of beer or four ounces of wine can impair flying skills.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 2, “Mitigating Risk”, p. 2-8
notes.evidence: Alcohol—Have I been drinking within 8 hours?

notes.front: Before a flight, you check the aircraft thoroughly but do not ask yourself any questions. Which part of the preflight assessment have you skipped?
notes.back: B) The pilot self-assessment, such as the IMSAFE checklist.
notes.choices:
A) The airworthiness check
B) The pilot self-assessment, such as the IMSAFE checklist
C) Nothing: the aircraft check covers the pilot

notes.front: Which operational pitfall is poor decision-making based on an emotional response to other pilots rather than an objective look at the situation?
notes.back: Peer pressure.
notes.explanation: It is one of the classic behavioural traps the handbook lists in Figure 2-15.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 2, “Operational Pitfalls (Figure 2-15)”, p. 2-22
notes.evidence: Poor decision-making may be based upon an emotional response to peers, rather than evaluating a situation objectively.

notes.front: Which operational pitfall is trying to keep visual contact with the terrain at low altitude while instrument conditions exist?
notes.back: Scud running.
notes.explanation: It is one of the classic behavioural traps the handbook lists in Figure 2-15.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 2, “Operational Pitfalls (Figure 2-15)”, p. 2-22
notes.evidence: This occurs when a pilot tries to maintain visual contact with the terrain at low altitudes while instrument conditions exist.

notes.front: What can result when a pilot continues VFR into instrument conditions?
notes.back: Spatial disorientation, or collision with the ground or obstacles.
notes.explanation: It is even more dangerous if the pilot is not instrument rated or current.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 2, “Operational Pitfalls (Figure 2-15)”, p. 2-22
notes.evidence: Spatial disorientation or collision with ground/obstacles may occur when a pilot continues VFR into instrument conditions.

notes.front: Which operational pitfall shows itself as a constant state of surprise at what happens next?
notes.back: Getting behind the aircraft.
notes.explanation: It comes from letting events or the situation control the pilot’s actions; in extreme cases it leads to loss of positional or situational awareness.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 2, “Operational Pitfalls (Figure 2-15)”, p. 2-22
notes.evidence: A constant state of surprise at what happens next may be exhibited when the pilot is getting behind the aircraft.

notes.front: Which operational pitfall is relying on memory, regular skills and familiar routes instead of established procedures and published checklists?
notes.back: Neglect of flight planning, preflight inspections and checklists.
notes.explanation: The handbook notes this can be particularly true of experienced pilots.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 2, “Operational Pitfalls (Figure 2-15)”, p. 2-22
notes.evidence: A pilot may rely on short- and long-term memory, regular flying skills, and familiar routes instead of established procedures and published checklists.

notes.front: What are two examples of external pressures that can push a pilot to complete a flight at the expense of safety?
notes.back: Any two, for example someone waiting at the destination and the desire to impress someone.

notes.front: Heading home for a family event, you see the weather ahead worsening, but you press on because you promised to arrive and do not consider landing short. Which pitfall is this?
notes.back: A) Get-there-itis.
notes.choices:
A) Get-there-itis
B) Peer pressure
C) Flying outside the envelope
notes.choicesExplained: B: peer pressure is an emotional response to other pilots. C: flying outside the envelope is overestimating what the aircraft and your skills can do.
notes.explanation: Fixation on the original destination with disregard for alternatives is how the handbook describes get-there-itis.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 2, “Operational Pitfalls (Figure 2-15)”, p. 2-22
notes.evidence: This disposition impairs pilot judgment through a fixation on the original goal or destination, combined with a disregard for any alternative course of action.

notes.front: The cloud base lowers steadily and you descend to stay below it, following a road at low level while it drizzles. Which pitfall are you falling into?
notes.back: C) Scud running.
notes.choices:
A) Mindset
B) Getting behind the aircraft
C) Scud running
notes.choicesExplained: A: mindset is failing to recognise change; here the change is seen, but the response is to fly low. B: getting behind the aircraft is being constantly surprised by events.
notes.explanation: Trying to keep visual contact with the terrain at low altitude as instrument conditions close in is scud running.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 2, “Operational Pitfalls (Figure 2-15)”, p. 2-22
notes.evidence: This occurs when a pilot tries to maintain visual contact with the terrain at low altitudes while instrument conditions exist.

notes.front: Why should the after-landing checklist normally wait until the aeroplane has stopped beyond the runway holding position markings?
notes.back: To give full attention to controlling the aeroplane during the landing roll.
notes.explanation: Pilots dividing attention while moving have mistakenly retracted the landing gear instead of the flaps.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 2, “After-Landing”, p. 2-22
notes.evidence: To give full attention to controlling the airplane during the landing roll, the after-landing checklist should be performed only after the airplane is brought to a complete stop beyond the runway holding position markings.

notes.front: How does hyperventilation differ from hypoxia in cause and cure?
notes.back: Hypoxia: too little oxygen; cure is lower altitude and/or oxygen. Hyperventilation: too much carbon dioxide lost by overbreathing; cure is normal breathing.
notes.explanation: Many symptoms are similar, so it is important to diagnose and treat the right condition.
notes.source: Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), chapter 17, “Hyperventilation”, p. 17-4
notes.evidence: leading to abnormal loss of carbon dioxide from the blood.

notes.front: How does the leans differ from the graveyard spiral?
notes.back: The leans: after levelling from an unnoticed turn, you feel banked the other way. Graveyard spiral: in a prolonged turn, you feel level while descending.
notes.explanation: Both come from a turn the inner ear has stopped sensing; in the spiral, pulling back tightens the turn.
notes.source: Aeronautical Information Manual, chapter 8, section 1, “8-1-5 Illusions in Flight”
notes.evidence: An abrupt correction of a banked attitude, which has been entered too slowly to stimulate the motion sensing system in the inner ear, can create the illusion of banking in the opposite direction.
